 Title of Lecture: Lecture 7: Dynamical Systems 5

 Professor: Khalil Iskarous

 Section 1: The Harmonic Oscillator

   A harmonic oscillator is a dynamical system with two variables that feed into each other:
     position, written x , and velocity, written v . Position tells us where something is, and
     velocity tells us how fast and in which direction it is moving. The system is fully
     described by two rules of change, one for each variable, and each rule depends on the
     other variable.
        The dot above a letter is the notation for change over time. x˙ means the
          increase or decrease in x with time, so it is the rate at which position is
         changing at a given moment.
          In the same way, v˙ means the increase or decrease in v with time, so it is the
           rate at which velocity is changing.

    The first rule says that the rate of change of position is equal to the velocity:

                                                              x˙ = v

     This rule says that velocity drives position. When v is positive, x grows, and when v is
     negative, x shrinks. When v is exactly zero, x holds still for that instant.

     In the loop diagram, this is the red arrow running from v to x , which marks v as the cause
    and x as the thing being changed.

    The second rule says that the rate of change of velocity is equal to the negative of the
      position:

                                                                        v˙ = −x

     This rule says that position drives velocity, but with a minus sign. When x is positive,
     velocity is pushed downward, and when x is negative, velocity is pushed upward.

     This is the blue arrow running from x to v . Together, the red and blue arrows form a
     closed loop of mutual influence: v changes x , and x changes v , over and over.
   We can work out what this loop does by stepping through it by hand, starting from x = 1
    and v = 0 . At the very start, position is at its highest value and nothing is moving yet.
          Since x = 1 , the second rule gives v˙ = −1 , so velocity starts decreasing and
        becomes negative.
        Once v is negative, the first rule says x˙ is negative, so position begins to fall. It
             falls slowly at first, since v has only just started to become negative, and then
             falls faster and faster as v grows more negative.
          Position keeps falling until it crosses zero. At the moment x = 0 , the second
           rule gives v˙ = 0 , so velocity stops changing. This is the moment when velocity
             is at its most negative, which means position is falling at its fastest right as it
          passes through zero.
          After the crossing, x is negative, so v˙ = −x is now positive. Velocity starts
          climbing back toward zero, which means position is still falling but falling more
           slowly.
       When velocity reaches zero, position stops falling. This is the lowest point of x ,
           at −1 . From there, velocity turns positive, position starts to rise, and the whole
         sequence runs in reverse until x is back at +1 with v = 0 .

     Plotting both variables against time point by point gives two waves. Position starts at its
    peak of +1 , drops through zero, bottoms out at −1 , and comes back up to its peak.

Velocity starts at zero, dips negative, returns to zero, rises positive, and comes back to
     zero.

       The two waves are offset from each other by a quarter of a cycle. Velocity is zero
       whenever position is at a peak or a trough, and velocity is at its largest size
       whenever position is crossing zero.

         This offset is a direct consequence of the two rules. Position turns around only
       when velocity reaches zero, and velocity turns around only when position
         reaches zero.


Section 2: The Oscillation/Vibration Dynamical System

   An oscillation, also called a vibration, is a repeating back-and-forth motion around a
    central point. The two-variable loop between x and v is the basic dynamical system that
    produces it. Each variable pushes on the other, and the result is that neither one ever
     settles down.
      When the loop is drawn with one arrow from x to v and another from v back to
       x , it shows that the influence is circular. There is no single cause at the start and
       no single effect at the end.
        Graphed smoothly over time, x traces a wave that starts high, swings down
        below zero, swings back up, and continues this pattern through repeated cycles.
        v traces a wave of the same shape that starts at zero and heads negative first,
         staying a quarter cycle out of step with x .

   The key property of this system is that it never comes to rest on its own. In the systems
    from earlier dynamical-systems material, variables moved toward a resting value and
    stopped there. Here, every time one variable reaches its target, the other variable is at its
    largest value and pushes it past the target again.

         This is why the motion keeps repeating. Position overshoots zero because
          velocity is at its maximum at the moment position reaches zero.

         Velocity overshoots zero because position is at its maximum at the moment
          velocity reaches zero.


Section 3: Vibration Needs Two Physical Effects

    Physically, vibration requires two effects working together. Neither one alone can
    produce a back-and-forth motion.

   The first effect is a spring, more precisely a viscous spring. A spring is the springiness
    found in many objects around us, meaning their tendency to return to a natural shape or
    position after being pushed or pulled. The word "viscous" refers to a frictional, slowing
     quality, and it will be set aside here so that we can focus on the springiness itself.

      A spring has a property called stiffness. Stiffness measures how strongly the
         spring pulls back toward its natural position when it has been moved away from
               it.

      A very stiff spring pulls back hard, and a loose spring pulls back gently.

   The second effect is mass. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, and it determines
   how the object carries motion once it is moving.

    Vibration matters because it shows up across many different systems, both physical and
    abstract.

       The jolt we feel when a car hits a bump is a vibration. The car's suspension
         springs and the car's mass together produce a bouncing motion.

        Music is vibration. Strings, air columns, and drum skins all vibrate to produce
         sound.

      Boom and bust in economics is a vibration. An economy swings above and
        below a steady level in repeating cycles.

         Oscillation in SGD is a vibration. SGD stands for stochastic gradient descent,
        a method used to train machine-learning models by repeatedly nudging a value
        toward a target. Under some settings, that value swings back and forth around
         the target rather than settling onto it.

       The motion of the air in the vocal tract and the motion of the vocal folds
        during speech are vibrations. Every sound we produce when we talk is built
        from these vibrations.

Section 4: A Slice of Air in the Vocal Tract

   The air inside the vocal tract can be treated as a small slice of material made of many
     particles. During speech, the particles in the slice stay the same, and each particle stays
    the same size. What changes is the distance between the particles.

        At equilibrium spacing, the particles sit at their natural, resting distance from
        one another. A chosen pair of neighboring particles is at 100% of its
         equilibrium distance at this point.

       The equilibrium size of the slice serves as the reference that all other states are
        compared to.

   Compression is the state in which the particles are pushed closer together than their
    resting distance. In a compressed slice, the chosen pair of particles sits at only 56% of its
    equilibrium distance, and the whole slice shrinks.

       High pressure means air that is packed very close together. Compression is
         therefore a high-pressure state.

    Rarefaction is the state in which the particles are spread farther apart than their resting
    distance. In a rarefied slice, the chosen pair sits at 144% of its equilibrium distance, and
    the whole slice expands.

      Low pressure means air that is spread very far apart. Rarefaction is therefore
        a low-pressure state.

    During speech, a slice of air in the vocal tract alternates between compression and
    rarefaction, shrinking and expanding around its equilibrium size again and again. This
    alternation is a vibration of the air.

       The sizes used in this model are idealized and exaggerated so that the change in
         spacing is visible. Real air in the vocal tract changes its spacing by much
         smaller amounts.

When x is smaller, x˙ , its speed of falling, is smaller too. The spring moves quickly when
      it is far from its natural position and slows down as it gets closer.
      When graphed against time, x starts at 1 and curves downward toward zero.
       The slope of the curve is steeply negative at the start and becomes smaller and
         smaller negative as time goes on.

       The curve gets closer and closer to zero but never crosses it. There is nothing in
          this rule that could carry x past zero, since the speed shrinks to nothing as the
         distance shrinks to nothing.

      If the initial condition is negative, the same logic runs in the opposite direction. Starting
    below zero, x rises toward zero, quickly at first and then more and more slowly, with a
    slope that is smaller and smaller positive. It approaches zero from below and again
    never crosses it.

    This kind of system has a natural resting condition, which here is $x = 0**.** When the
    system's position is at a discrepancy with its natural position, meaning it has been moved
                                                                                   1   away from where it rests, it feeds back on itself through the rule x˙ = −  ​x to cancel that                                                                                   3
    discrepancy. This is the idea of negative feedback, also called balancing feedback, from
   Meadows' work on systems.

       The feedback is called negative because the change always opposes the
         discrepancy. A positive discrepancy produces a negative change, and a negative
         discrepancy produces a positive change.

            It is called balancing because its effect is to bring the system back into balance
          at its resting point.

   These are systems that are in motion only in order to achieve their equilibrium. An
    equilibrium is a state where the system has no reason to change any further. A spring
   moves only because it is away from its natural position, and once it arrives there, all
    motion stops.
                     1   The number −  in the rule is what we call stiffness. Its size controls how quickly the                                    ​3
    spring returns to equilibrium.

      A higher stiffness, such as a larger fraction than one third, means the spring
         closes a bigger share of the remaining distance at every step, so it returns to
         zero faster.

      A lower stiffness, such as a smaller fraction than one third, means the spring
         closes a smaller share of the remaining distance at every step, so it returns to
         zero more slowly.


Section 6: Mass and Persistent Motion

   Mass behaves very differently from a spring. If a mass is moving, it just keeps on
    moving. A mass does not need a discrepancy or a target to keep going, and it has no
    natural resting position that it is trying to reach.

    This principle was worked out by Galileo, Descartes, and Newton: a mass in motion
    stays in motion. Without an outside force acting on it, a moving object continues at the
   same speed in the same direction.

        Motion of this kind is called constant velocity. An object with constant velocity
         covers the same distance in every equal interval of time.

      A car rolling along a straight street past buildings and trees at constant velocity
       moves past the same amount of scenery in every moment. It does not speed up,
        slow down, or stop on its own.

    This property is exactly what the spring lacks. A spring slows down as it nears its resting
    point and stops there, while a mass carries its motion forward regardless of where it is.


Section 7: A Spring Stops at a Place, a Mass Stops After a Process

   The difference between the two effects can be stated in one line: a spring stops at a place,
    while a mass stops after a process. The spring's stopping point is a location, its natural
    position. A mass does not stop at a location at all, and it keeps moving until something
   removes its motion over time.

    Consider a spring attached to a wall on one end, lying on a table, with no mass on its free
    end. Its displacement x is measured from the spring's natural position, which is set as
   x = 0 , and the scale runs from −1 to +1 .

When the free end is pulled out to +1 and released, the spring returns and
         stops at x = 0 . The end approaches zero without crossing it.
        Graphed over time, this return from +1 is a curve that starts at +1 and bends
       down toward zero, flattening out as it gets close. It has the same shape as the
                                        1
        curve produced by x˙ = − 3 ​x .
      When the free end is instead pushed to −1 and released, x rises toward zero
        without crossing it. The curve starts at −1 and bends up toward zero, again
          flattening as it arrives.

         Pulling the spring out again gives the exact same return each time. A spring
         alone always settles at its natural position and never overshoots.

   When a mass is attached to the free end of the same spring and the system is released
    from +1 , the result is completely different. The spring still pulls the mass back toward
     zero, but when the mass reaches zero it is moving at its fastest, and the mass carries that
   motion through the crossing.

       The mass continues past zero into negative displacement. Now the spring is
         stretched the other way, so it pulls back toward zero from the negative side. The
       mass slows down, stops near −1 , and is pulled back through zero toward the
          positive side again.

         This repeats through every crossing. The mass keeps going back and forth past
         the natural position rather than stopping at it.

   Graphed over time, the spring-plus-mass system produces a lightly damped oscillation.
   The curve swings from +1 down below zero, back up above zero, and continues swinging
    through repeated cycles.

       Damping is the gradual loss of motion over time, which comes from the
          viscous, frictional part of the spring. In a lightly damped system, the damping is
          small, so each swing is only a little smaller than the one before it and the
          oscillation continues for many cycles.

         Eventually, the damping would bring the mass to rest at zero, which is what it
       means for a mass to stop after a process. The stopping happens only at the end
          of a long sequence of swings.

    Putting the two effects together recovers the harmonic oscillator. The spring supplies the
    pull back toward the natural position, which is the rule v˙ = −x : the farther the mass is
    from zero, the harder its velocity is pushed back toward zero. The mass supplies
    persistent motion, which is the rule x˙ = v : position keeps changing as long as there is
     velocity, including at the moment the mass passes through zero.

      A spring alone gives balancing feedback that ends at equilibrium.

      A mass alone gives motion that never turns around.

      A spring and a mass together give vibration, since the spring keeps turning
         the motion around and the mass keeps carrying it past the resting point.

Section 8: A Cosine in the Vocal Tract

   The vibration of a slice of air in the vocal tract can be described with a single
    mathematical function, the cosine. The value x here measures the normalized
    expansion of the slice, meaning how far the particles are spread relative to their
    equilibrium spacing, scaled so that the extremes are +1 and −1 .

                           x = cos(phase)

   x = +1 means the particles are farthest apart, which is maximum rarefaction.
   x = 0 means the particles are at their equilibrium spacing.
   x = −1 means the particles are closest together, which is maximum compression.

   The phase is the input to the cosine, and it tracks where the slice is within its cycle of
    motion. One full cycle of the cosine takes a phase of 2π , so a phase running from 0 to 6π
    covers exactly three cycles.
        At a phase of 0 , the cosine equals +1 , so the slice starts at maximum
          rarefaction.

At a phase of π , the cosine equals −1 , so the slice has reached maximum
        compression halfway through the first cycle.
        At a phase of 2π , the cosine is back at +1 , so the slice has returned to maximum
          rarefaction and completed Cycle 1. The same pattern repeats for Cycle 2, ending
          at 4π , and Cycle 3, ending at 6π .

   The slice therefore moves from maximum rarefaction to compression and back to
    rarefaction in every cycle, following the cosine curve exactly.
        Partway through a swing, the slice is in an in-between state. At x = +0.84 , the
          particles are still rarefied, farther apart than at equilibrium but not at their
      maximum spread. At x = −0.84 , the particles are compressed, closer together
        than at equilibrium but not at their tightest.

    This cosine is the same wave that position traced in the harmonic oscillator, starting at its
   peak and swinging down through zero to its lowest point and back. The air in the vocal
     tract behaves as a harmonic oscillator, with the springiness of the air pushing it back
    toward equilibrium spacing and the mass of the air carrying it past equilibrium each time.

       The sizes of the slice in this model are exaggerated and its motion is slowed, so
         that each stage of the cycle is visible. The dashed boundary marks the slice's
         equilibrium size.


Section 9: Vowels and Tongue Position

    Different vowels are made by placing the tongue in different positions inside the vocal
     tract. Side-view MRI images of the head during five words show how the tongue body
   moves to create each vowel. The vowels are organized along two dimensions: height,
   which is how high or low the tongue body sits in the mouth, and front/back, which is how
     far forward or backward the tongue body sits.

   High vowels are made with the tongue body raised close to the roof of the mouth.

         In "dean," the vowel is high and front. The tongue body is pushed up and
        forward toward the hard palate, which leaves a wide open space in the throat
        behind the tongue.

         In "dune," the vowel is high and back. The tongue body is raised but bunched
        toward the back of the mouth, closer to the soft palate.

   Low vowels are made with the tongue body lowered away from the roof of the mouth.

         In "Dan," the vowel is low and front. The tongue sits lower in the mouth while
         staying toward the front, leaving a large open space above it.

         In "Don," the vowel is low and back. The tongue is lowered and pulled back
        toward the throat, which narrows the space behind the tongue.

    In "done," the vowel is central. The tongue body sits in a middle position, neither pushed
     far forward nor pulled far back.

   Each tongue position gives the air inside the vocal tract a different shape. A different
    shape changes how the air vibrates, and those differences in vibration are what make one
    vowel sound different from another.


Section 10: One Time Interval, Three Frequencies

   The frequency of a vibration is how many complete cycles it goes through in a given
   amount of time. Three vibrations can be compared over the same 12-second interval, with
    each one covering the same range of particle spacing and each one starting at maximum
    rarefaction, where x = +1 .
       x = +1 is maximum rarefaction, x = 0 is equilibrium, and x = −1 is
      maximum compression, just as in the single cosine.

   The low-frequency vibration completes 3 cycles in 12 seconds. Each cycle takes 4
    seconds, so its peaks at +1 fall at 0, 4, 8, and 12 seconds. Measured in cycles per second,
     its frequency is:

    All three vibrations reach the same extremes of rarefaction and compression. The only
    thing that differs among them is how quickly the cycle repeats. Frequency is therefore
    a separate property from how far the particles spread or squeeze, and a vibration can be
   made faster or slower without changing its range.

       One cycle per second is called one hertz, written Hz. This unit is used for the
         frequencies in the vowel models.


Section 11: Vowels as Combined Vibrations

   A vowel is not a single cosine. A vowel can be modeled as a sum of vibrations at different
    frequencies happening at the same time in the same slice of air. The simplest model
    uses two frequencies of equal size added together, and the two frequencies chosen give
    each vowel its own pattern of motion.

       The frequencies in these models are small illustrative values, chosen so the
        combined wave is easy to follow. They are not the actual frequencies found in
         speech.
   A cosine at a frequency of f Hz can be written as cos(2πft) , where t is time in seconds.
    Since one cycle takes a phase of 2π , multiplying 2π by f gives f full cycles for every
    second that passes.
      A 1 Hz vibration is cos(2πt) , which reaches a phase of 2π , or one full cycle, at
          t = 1 second.
      A 4 Hz vibration is cos(8πt) , which reaches a phase of 8π , or four full cycles, at
          t = 1 second.

   The vowel /i/, the vowel in "dean," is modeled as a 1 Hz vibration plus a 4 Hz vibration:

                              x(t) = cos(2πt) + cos(8πt)

    At t = 0 , both cosines equal +1 , so the sum is:

                                x(0) = 1 + 1 = 2

    This means the combined wave starts at +2 , which is maximum rarefaction for the
   combined motion. The range of x is now from +2 to −2 , since two waves of size 1 are
    stacked together.
    At t = 0.5 seconds, the 1 Hz wave is halfway through its cycle and the 4 Hz wave has
    completed exactly two cycles, so the sum is:

                       x(0.5) = cos(π) + cos(4π) = −1 + 1 = 0

   Between its large peaks, the /i/ wave has a busy pattern: it rises to smaller peaks near +1 ,
    dips down to troughs near −1.7 , and touches zero at the halfway point. The fast 4 Hz
   wave rides on top of the slow 1 Hz wave, putting several smaller wiggles inside each slow
     cycle.
   The whole pattern repeats once every second, returning to +2 at 1, 2, and 3 seconds.

   The vowel /a/, close to the vowel in "Don," is modeled as a 2 Hz vibration plus a 3 Hz
    vibration:

                              x(t) = cos(4πt) + cos(6πt)

    At t = 0 , both cosines equal +1 , so /a/ also starts at x = +2 , which is maximum
    rarefaction.
    At t = 0.5 seconds, the 2 Hz wave has completed exactly one cycle and the 3 Hz wave has
    completed one and a half cycles, so the sum is:

x(0.5) = cos(2π) + cos(3π) = 1 + (−1) = 0

   The /a/ wave has a different shape from /i/. Between each large peak at +2 , it drops to a
   deep trough near −1.6 , rises to a pair of small humps near +0.7 separated by a dip down
    to zero, drops to another deep trough, and returns to +2 .
    This pattern also repeats once every second, returning to +2 at 1, 2, and 3 seconds.
    In both vowels, positive x means rarefaction and negative x means compression. Both
    vowels start at the same value and repeat at the same rate, yet the air moves in a clearly
    different way within each second. The combination of frequencies is what
    distinguishes one vowel from another.

       The motion in these models is played back at one quarter of its speed so that the
          particle spacing can be followed.


Section 12: Perturbation Theory

    Perturbation theory is the study of how a system's behavior changes when one of its
    parameters is nudged up or down. A parameter is a fixed setting of a system, such as how
    heavy the mass is or how stiff the spring is. For a mass-spring system, the behavior of
    interest is its frequency, meaning how many oscillations it completes per second.
     If we increase the mass m of a mass-spring system, the frequency decreases.

      A heavier mass carries its motion more strongly, so the spring takes longer to
        slow it down and turn it around at each end of its swing.

        Each cycle therefore takes longer, and fewer cycles fit into each second. More
       mass means a lower frequency.
     If we increase the stiffness k of the spring, the frequency increases.

      A stiffer spring pulls back harder on the mass for the same displacement, so it
         turns the mass around more quickly at each end of its swing.

        Each cycle therefore takes less time, and more cycles fit into each second. More
          stiffness means a higher frequency.

    These two results together form the core perturbation-theory relationships for a mass-
    spring system:

         Increasing mass lowers frequency.

         Increasing stiffness raises frequency.

        These relationships give us a way to predict how a vibrating system will sound
         or behave just from knowing whether it is heavy or light and stiff or loose.


Section 13: Hearing Explained

   The mass-spring relationships explain how the ear separates sounds by frequency. This
    explanation comes from the work of Georg von Békésy, who received the Nobel Prize in
    1961 for discovering how the inner ear responds to sound.

    Inside the inner ear is a long, tapered membrane called the basilar membrane. It is wide
     at one end and narrow at the other, and its physical properties change gradually along its
    length.
        At the wide end, the membrane has large mass M and small stiffness k . It is
        heavy and loose.
        At the narrow end, the membrane has small mass m and large stiffness K . It
            is light and stiff.

       Moving along the membrane from the wide end to the narrow end, mass
          steadily decreases and stiffness steadily increases.

    Applying perturbation theory to each location on the membrane gives each location its
   own preferred frequency.

        At the wide end, large mass lowers the frequency and small stiffness also lowers
         the frequency. This end vibrates most strongly for low-frequency sounds.

        At the narrow end, small mass raises the frequency and large stiffness also
          raises the frequency. This end vibrates most strongly for high-frequency
         sounds.

        Every point in between has an intermediate mass and stiffness, so every point is
        tuned to an intermediate frequency. The membrane is effectively a long row of

mass-spring systems, each set to a slightly different frequency.

   Nerve fibers leave the membrane at many different locations along its length. When a
    particular spot on the membrane vibrates, the fibers at that spot become active, and
   which fibers are active tells the brain which frequencies are present in the sound.

      When a vowel made of two combined frequencies reaches the ear, such as the 1
       Hz and 4 Hz combination for /i/, two different places along the membrane
          vibrate, one for each frequency. The membrane separates the combined
         vibration back into its component frequencies.

         This is how the ear can tell /i/ from /a/: the two vowels are built from different
        frequency combinations, so they set different places on the membrane into
          vibration.


Section 14: The Fundamental Learning Tradeoff

    In machine learning, a model is trained by repeatedly updating a value to move it toward
    a target. The learning rate, written γ , sets how large each update is, as a fraction of the
    remaining distance to the target. Each full round of updates through the training data is
    called an epoch.
   The effect of γ can be seen by training three runs that start at very different values, one
    near 130, one near 80, and one near 10, and all head toward a target of about 80. Each run
     is tracked over 300 epochs at four different learning rates.

        At a learning rate of 1%, the runs move smoothly and slowly. The run starting
          at 130 curves down gradually and is still at about 82 after 300 epochs. The run
          starting at 10 curves up gradually and has only reached about 76 after 300
         epochs. The motion is very steady, but the runs have not fully reached the
          target even by the end.

        At a learning rate of 10%, the runs reach the neighborhood of 80 within
         roughly the first 30 to 50 epochs. After arriving, they stay close to 80 with small
         wiggles of a few units above and below.

        At a learning rate of 50%, the runs jump to the region of 80 within just a few
         epochs. After that, they bounce around noisily, swinging roughly between 70
        and 95 rather than sitting on the target.

        At a learning rate of 80%, the runs reach the target region almost immediately,
        but they bounce even more widely, roughly between 68 and 97, for all 300
         epochs.

    These results show the fundamental learning tradeoff:
      When γ increases, speed increases and accuracy decreases. Large updates
         get the value to the target region quickly, but the same large updates keep
        throwing the value past the target, so it oscillates around the answer instead of
          settling on it.
      When γ decreases, speed decreases and accuracy increases. Small updates
        keep the value on a smooth, steady path with very little bouncing, but they take
       many more epochs to arrive.

         This is the oscillation in SGD that appears among the everyday examples of
          vibration. A high learning rate turns training into a back-and-forth swinging
        motion around the target.

   The tradeoff is an unfortunate one, since in practice we want both fast learning and
    accurate learning at the same time. Thousands of people, over generations, have made
    their living by finding better ways to optimize, meaning better training methods that
    raise both speed and accuracy together rather than trading one against the other.

       The goal of this work is a method where speed increases and accuracy
         increases at once, escaping the tradeoff that a single fixed learning rate forces
       on us.

Section 1: The Harmonic Oscillator

   A harmonic oscillator is a dynamical system built from two variables that drive each
    other: position, written x , and velocity, written v . The dot above a letter marks change
    over time, so x˙ means the increase or decrease in x with time, and v˙ means the increase
    or decrease in v with time. Each variable has its own rule of change, and each rule
   depends on the other variable.

   The first rule says that position changes at a rate equal to the velocity:

                                                             x˙ = v

    Velocity drives position. When v is positive, x grows, when v is negative, x shrinks, and
   when v is zero, x holds still for that instant.

   The second rule says that velocity changes at a rate equal to the negative of the position:

                                                                      v˙ = −x

    Position drives velocity, but with a minus sign. A positive x pushes velocity downward,
   and a negative x pushes velocity upward.
    Together the two rules form a closed loop of mutual influence, where v changes x and x
    changes v over and over.
    Stepping through the loop by hand from x = 1 and v = 0 shows how it produces
    repeating motion.
        With x = 1 , the second rule gives v˙ = −1 , so velocity becomes negative.
       Once v is negative, the first rule makes x˙ negative, so position starts to fall. It
           falls slowly at first and then faster as v grows more negative.
      When position reaches x = 0 , the second rule gives v˙ = 0 , so velocity stops
         changing. Velocity is at its most negative at this moment, which means position
            is falling fastest as it passes through zero.
       Once x is negative, v˙ is positive, so velocity climbs back toward zero and
         position falls more slowly.
      When velocity reaches zero, position stops falling at its lowest point, −1 .
         Velocity then turns positive, position rises, and the whole sequence runs in
         reverse until x is back at +1 with v = 0 .
    Plotted against time, both variables trace waves. Position starts at its peak of +1 , drops
    through zero to −1 , and returns to its peak. Velocity starts at zero, dips negative, returns
    to zero, rises positive, and returns to zero.

       The two waves are offset by a quarter of a cycle. Velocity is zero whenever
         position is at a peak or trough, and velocity is largest whenever position
         crosses zero.

         This offset follows directly from the two rules, since position turns around only
       when velocity reaches zero, and velocity turns around only when position
         reaches zero.


Section 2: The Oscillation/Vibration Dynamical System

   An oscillation, also called a vibration, is a repeating back-and-forth motion around a
    central point. The two-variable loop between x and v is the dynamical system that
    produces it. The influence runs in a circle, with x acting on v and v acting back on x , so
    there is no single starting cause and no single final effect.
        Over time, x traces a smooth wave that starts high, swings below zero, swings
        back up, and repeats. v traces a wave of the same shape that starts at zero, heads
         negative first, and stays a quarter cycle out of step with x .

This system never comes to rest on its own. Every time one variable reaches zero, the
    other variable is at its largest value and pushes it past zero again.

         Position overshoots zero since velocity is at its maximum at the moment
         position reaches zero.

         Velocity overshoots zero since position is at its maximum at the moment
          velocity reaches zero.


Section 3: Vibration Needs Two Physical Effects

    Vibration requires two physical effects working together.

   The first effect is a viscous spring, which is the springiness found in many things around
     us, meaning their tendency to return to a natural position after being moved. The word
    "viscous" refers to a frictional, slowing quality and is set aside here. A spring has a
    property called stiffness, which measures how strongly it pulls back toward its natural
    position.

   The second effect is mass, which determines how an object carries motion once it is
    moving.

    Vibration appears across many different systems.

            It is what we feel when a car hits a bump.

            It is music.

            It is boom and bust in economics, where an economy swings above and below
        a steady level in repeating cycles.

            It is oscillation in SGD. SGD stands for stochastic gradient descent, a method
          for training machine-learning models by repeatedly updating a value toward a
          target, and under some settings that value swings back and forth around the
          target.

            It is the motion of the air in the vocal tract and the motion of the vocal folds
        during speech.


Section 4: A Slice of Air in the Vocal Tract

   A slice of air in the vocal tract is made of many particles. During vibration, the particles
    stay the same and each one stays the same size, but the distances between them
    change.

        At equilibrium spacing, the particles sit at their resting distance. A chosen pair
          of neighboring particles is at 100% of its equilibrium distance.

         In compression, the particles are pushed closer together, and the chosen pair
         shrinks to 56% of its equilibrium distance. High pressure means air packed
        very close together, so compression is a high-pressure state.

         In rarefaction, the particles spread farther apart, and the chosen pair stretches
          to 144% of its equilibrium distance. Low pressure means air spread very far
         apart, so rarefaction is a low-pressure state.

   A vibrating slice of air alternates between compression and rarefaction, shrinking and
    expanding around its equilibrium size. In this idealized model, the slice's equilibrium size
    serves as the reference, and the motion is exaggerated so the change in spacing is visible.

Section 6: Mass and Persistent Motion

     If a mass is moving, it just keeps on moving. A mass has no natural resting position that
      it is trying to reach and needs no discrepancy to keep going.

    Galileo, Descartes, and Newton established that a mass in motion stays in motion. A
   mass moving at constant velocity covers the same distance in every equal interval of
    time, without speeding up, slowing down, or stopping on its own. A spring slows as it
    nears its resting point and stops there, while a mass carries its motion forward regardless
    of where it is.


Section 7: A Spring Stops at a Place, a Mass Stops After a Process

  A spring stops at a place, while a mass stops after a process. The spring's stopping point
     is a location, its natural position, while a moving mass continues until its motion is
   removed over time.
    For a spring attached to a wall with no mass, displacement x is measured from the
    spring's natural position at x = 0 , on a scale from −1 to +1 .
         Pulled to +1 and released, the spring returns and stops at x = 0 , approaching
         zero without crossing it. Over time, this return is a curve that bends down from
      +1 and flattens as it reaches zero.
        Pushed to −1 and released, the spring rises toward zero without crossing it,
         following a curve that bends up and flattens.

        Repeating the pull gives the same return every time, since a spring alone always
          settles at its natural position.
   With a mass attached and the system released from +1 , the spring pulls the mass toward
     zero, but the mass is moving fastest when it reaches zero and carries its motion through
    the crossing.

       The mass continues into negative displacement, where the spring pulls it back
        toward zero from the other side. It slows, stops near −1 , and is pulled back
        through zero toward the positive side.

The mass carries motion through every crossing, so it keeps swinging back
        and forth past the natural position.

   Over time, the spring-plus-mass system produces a lightly damped oscillation, a curve
    that swings from +1 below zero, back above zero, and on through repeated cycles.
   Damping is the gradual loss of motion from the viscous part of the spring. When
   damping is light, each swing is only slightly smaller than the one before, so the mass
    stops only after a long process of swings.

   The two effects together form the harmonic oscillator. The spring's pull toward the
    natural position corresponds to v˙ = −x , and the mass's persistent motion corresponds to
      x˙ = v .

      A spring alone gives balancing feedback that ends at equilibrium.

      A mass alone gives motion that never turns around.

      A spring and a mass together give vibration, since the spring keeps turning
         the motion around and the mass keeps carrying it past the resting point.


Section 8: A Cosine in the Vocal Tract

   The vibration of a slice of air in the vocal tract follows a cosine. Here x measures the
    normalized expansion of the slice, scaled so its extremes are +1 and −1 :

                           x = cos(phase)

   x = +1 means the particles are farthest apart, which is maximum rarefaction.
   x = 0 means the particles are at equilibrium spacing.
   x = −1 means the particles are closest together, which is maximum compression.
   The phase tracks where the slice is within its cycle, and one full cycle takes a phase of 2π .
   A phase from 0 to 6π therefore covers three cycles.
        At phase 0 , x = +1 , so the slice starts at maximum rarefaction.
        At phase π , x = −1 , so the slice reaches maximum compression halfway
        through Cycle 1.
        At phase 2π , x returns to +1 , completing Cycle 1. Cycle 2 ends at 4π and Cycle
        3 ends at 6π .

    In every cycle, the slice moves from maximum rarefaction to compression and back to
    rarefaction. In between the extremes, x = +0.84 is a rarefied state with particles farther
    apart than equilibrium but not at their widest, and x = −0.84 is a compressed state with
    particles closer than equilibrium but not at their tightest.

         This cosine has the same shape as the position wave of the harmonic oscillator,
          starting at its peak and swinging through zero to its lowest point and back.


Section 9: Vowels and Tongue Position

    Vowels differ in where the tongue body sits inside the vocal tract, along two dimensions.
    Height is how high or low the tongue body sits, and front/back is how far forward or
   backward it sits.

   High vowels have the tongue body raised toward the roof of the mouth.

         In "dean," the vowel is high and front. The tongue body is raised and pushed
         forward, leaving a wide space behind the tongue.

         In "dune," the vowel is high and back. The tongue body is raised and bunched
        toward the back of the mouth.

   Low vowels have the tongue body lowered away from the roof of the mouth.

         In "Dan," the vowel is low and front. The tongue sits low while staying forward,
         leaving a large open space above it.

         In "Don," the vowel is low and back. The tongue is lowered and pulled back,
        narrowing the space behind it.

    In "done," the vowel is central, with the tongue body in a middle position that is neither
     far forward nor far back.

Section 11: Vowels as Combined Vibrations

   A vowel can be modeled as two vibrations at different frequencies added together in
    the same slice of air, with equal component amplitudes. These are illustrative two-
    frequency models, and the pair of frequencies gives each vowel its own pattern of motion.
      A cosine at f Hz can be written as cos(2πft) , where t is time in seconds. One
         cycle takes a phase of 2π , so cos(2πt) completes one cycle per second and
        cos(8πt) completes four.

   The vowel /i/ is modeled as 1 Hz + 4 Hz:

                              x(t) = cos(2πt) + cos(8πt)

    At t = 0 , both cosines equal +1 :

                                x(0) = 1 + 1 = 2

   The combined wave starts at +2 , which is maximum rarefaction, and its range runs from
   +2 to −2 .
    At t = 0.5 seconds:

                       x(0.5) = cos(π) + cos(4π) = −1 + 1 = 0

    Within each second, the fast 4 Hz wave rides on the slow 1 Hz wave. The /i/ wave drops
    from +2 to troughs near −1.7 , rises to smaller peaks near +1 , touches zero at the
    halfway point, and returns to +2 at 1, 2, and 3 seconds.

   The vowel /a/ is modeled as 2 Hz + 3 Hz:

                              x(t) = cos(4πt) + cos(6πt)

    At t = 0 , both cosines equal +1 , so /a/ also starts at x = +2 , maximum rarefaction.
    At t = 0.5 seconds:

                     x(0.5) = cos(2π) + cos(3π) = 1 + (−1) = 0

    Within each second, the /a/ wave drops from +2 to a deep trough near −1.6 , rises to two
    small humps near +0.7 separated by a dip to zero, drops to another deep trough, and
    returns to +2 at 1, 2, and 3 seconds.
    In both models, positive x means rarefaction and negative x means compression, and
    the motion is played back at one quarter speed. Both vowels start at +2 and repeat once

per second, but the air moves in a different pattern within each second, and that pattern
     is set by the combination of frequencies.


Section 12: Perturbation Theory

    Perturbation theory asks how a system's behavior changes when one of its settings is
    increased or decreased. For a mass-spring system, the behavior is its frequency.
     If the mass m increases, the frequency decreases. A heavier mass carries its motion
   more strongly, so the spring takes longer to turn it around at each end of its swing, and
    fewer cycles fit into each second.
     If the stiffness k increases, the frequency increases. A stiffer spring pulls back harder at
    the same displacement, so it turns the mass around more quickly, and more cycles fit into
    each second.

   The two perturbation relationships are that increasing mass lowers frequency and
    increasing stiffness raises frequency.


Section 13: Hearing Explained

   Georg von Békésy received the Nobel Prize in 1961 for explaining hearing using these
   mass and stiffness relationships.

    Hearing depends on a long, tapered membrane in the ear whose mass and stiffness
   change gradually along its length.
        At the wide end, the membrane has large mass M and small stiffness k , so it is
        heavy and loose.
        At the narrow end, it has small mass m and large stiffness K , so it is light and
             stiff.

       Moving from the wide end to the narrow end, mass steadily decreases and
          stiffness steadily increases.

    Applying perturbation theory gives each location its own frequency.

        At the wide end, large mass and small stiffness both lower the frequency, so this
        end vibrates for low frequencies.

        At the narrow end, small mass and large stiffness both raise the frequency, so
          this end vibrates for high frequencies.

        Each point in between has intermediate mass and stiffness, so it vibrates for an
         intermediate frequency.

    Fibers leave the membrane at many points along its length. The location that vibrates
    determines which fibers carry a signal, so the place of vibration along the membrane
   encodes the frequency of the sound.


Section 14: The Fundamental Learning Tradeoff

    In training, a value is updated repeatedly toward a target, and the learning rate, written
   γ , sets how large each update is. Each full round of training updates is an epoch.

    Three runs starting near 130, near 80, and near 10 all move toward a target of about 80
    over 300 epochs, and the learning rate changes how they get there.

        At a learning rate of 1%, the runs move smoothly and slowly. After 300 epochs,
         the run from 130 is still near 82 and the run from 10 has reached only about 76.

        At a learning rate of 10%, the runs reach the region of 80 within roughly the
            first 30 to 50 epochs and then stay near it with small wiggles.

        At a learning rate of 50%, the runs reach 80 within a few epochs but then
        bounce noisily, roughly between 70 and 95.

        At a learning rate of 80%, the runs reach the target region almost immediately
        but bounce even more widely, roughly between 68 and 97, for all 300 epochs.

    These results define the fundamental learning tradeoff.
      When γ increases, speed increases and accuracy decreases. Large updates
         reach the target region quickly, but they keep overshooting, so the value
          oscillates around the target instead of settling on it. This is the oscillation in
       SGD.
      When γ decreases, speed decreases and accuracy increases. Small updates
         follow a smooth, steady path with little bouncing, but they need many more

epochs to arrive.

The tradeoff is unwelcome, since fast and accurate learning are both wanted at once.
Thousands of people for generations have made their living by finding better ways to
optimize, so that speed increases and accuracy increases together.
